passage: Exam week, and a power cut had shut the hostel mess early. Baljeet didn't mind. For months she had kept private rules: no food until every chapter was revised, only the same plain things, never in front of anyone. When her marks slipped or her father's calls turned sharp, the rules felt like the one thing she could control. Skipping felt clean, almost calm, for an hour. Then, on the stairs before the chemistry paper, the walls tilted and she sat down hard. Afreen from the next room crouched beside her. "This isn't the first time, is it?" Baljeet shook her head. After the paper, Afreen walked her to the campus health centre. Baljeet had planned to say "just tired". Instead she told the doctor about the rules. The doctor listened without scolding and referred her to a specialist.

qa.q: What was Baljeet's rule about revising?
qa.a: No food until every chapter was revised.

qa.q: Why did the rules feel good to Baljeet at first?
qa.a: When her marks slipped or her father's calls turned sharp, she felt out of control, and the rules gave her a brief sense of calm and control.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the health centre?
qa.a: Baljeet had planned to say "just tired" but chose to tell the doctor about the rules, which led to a referral to a specialist.

qa.q: How might Afreen see what happened on the stairs?
qa.a: Afreen likely saw it as part of a pattern, not a one-off, which is why Afreen asked if it was the first time and walked Baljeet to the health centre.

grounding: It shows a young adult using strict secret food rules to cope with stress and a need for control, getting brief relief and real harm, and turning to a doctor.

passage: After the team lead snapped at her in front of everyone, Dilnaz took the lift down to the office basement with a plastic bag of snacks bought on her break. She ate fast on the stairwell, without tasting anything. For ten minutes the noise in her head went quiet. Then came the heavy stomach, the shame, the wrappers pushed deep into the dustbin under other rubbish so nobody would see. It had happened four evenings this week. Back at the flat she told Damini, her flatmate, that she wasn't hungry, and skipped dinner, the way she always did afterwards. That night Damini found her awake at two. Dilnaz meant to say nothing. Instead she said, "I think I'm using food to get through the day, and it's hurting me." Damini didn't laugh or lecture. She held out her phone. "Let's book the doctor for Saturday. I'll come with you."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz push the wrappers?
qa.a: Deep into the dustbin under other rubbish.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz feel during the ten minutes of eating, and afterwards?
qa.a: A brief quiet relief while eating, then a heavy stomach and shame.

qa.q: Which choice at two in the morning changed things?
qa.a: Dilnaz named what was happening to Damini instead of staying silent, and Damini helped book a doctor for Saturday.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Dilnaz finally speaks?
qa.a: Damini may be worried but glad to be trusted, and shows it by not laughing or lecturing and offering to come along.

grounding: It shows a young adult using secret eating to cope with stress and shame, feeling brief relief and real harm, and starting with a doctor.

College counsellor's note, Tuesday.
Vikas, nineteen, was brought in by his roommate after he nearly fainted in the chemistry lab. Over several sessions I've learnt that for months he has kept strict food rules: the same few foods at exactly the same times, and skipping meals entirely before exams. When the mess changed its menu last week, he panicked and didn't eat that day.
He told me, "When everything else is out of control, this is the one thing I can control. It makes me feel calm for a bit." Then he admitted he feels dizzy, cold and ashamed most days.
I told him this relief is real but so is the harm, and that this needs a doctor first. With his agreement, I booked him with the college doctor and informed his parents. — Gargi

qa.q: Where did Vikas nearly faint?
qa.a: In the chemistry lab.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel about his food rules?
qa.a: They make him feel calm and in control for a while, but he also feels dizzy, cold and ashamed most days.

qa.q: What did Gargi do that was the right place to start?
qa.a: Gargi explained the relief was real but so was the harm, booked him with the college doctor and informed his parents with his agreement.

qa.q: How might Vikas's roommate have felt seeing him nearly faint?
qa.a: The roommate was probably frightened and concerned, which is why he brought Vikas in.

grounding: Shows a young adult using rigid food rules to cope with stress and a need for control, getting brief relief and real harm, and a counsellor pointing him to a doctor.

passage:
Thursday
Exam week. I did the rules again today. Same breakfast, nothing till evening, then only what's on the list. It makes the panic about exams go quiet for a while, like I'm in charge of something.
But I was dizzy on the stairs. My hands are always cold. I hide what I'm doing, even from Lalit, and he's my brother, I tell him everything.
Tonight Lalit sat at the end of my bed. He said, "I've noticed you're not eating with us. I'm not angry. I'm scared for you." I cried and told him some of it.
He said, "This isn't something you can fix alone." He's right. Tomorrow we're going to the doctor together. I've already told Mummy.
Arohi

qa.q: Who sat at the end of the bed?
qa.a: Lalit, Arohi's brother.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel when following the food rules?
qa.a: Arohi feels briefly calmer and in charge during exam panic, but also dizzy, cold and secretive.

qa.q: What step is Arohi taking, and why is it right?
qa.a: Seeing a doctor with Lalit, because the food rules bring real harm and a doctor is the right place to start.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about what he noticed?
qa.a: Lalit felt scared for Arohi, though he made clear he was not angry.

passage:
In his final year at the college in Sangli, Deepak's father fell ill, the exams moved up, and everything felt out of his hands. Food became the one thing he could control.
He made rules. No eating before evening. Only certain foods. He ate in secret, alone, then felt ashamed. When he followed his rules, he felt a rush of relief, calm, almost proud.
But he was dizzy at cricket practice. He couldn't focus in class. He snapped at his sister Reena when she put a plate in front of him.
One evening Reena found him sitting on the steps, pale. "I'm not going to fight about food," she said quietly. "I'm scared for you. Let's see the doctor at the district hospital tomorrow."
Deepak stared at the ground. "It's the only thing that feels in my control."
"I know. The doctor can help with that too." He nodded.

qa.q: Where did Deepak feel dizzy?
qa.a: At cricket practice.

qa.q: Why did following his food rules feel good to Deepak?
qa.a: He felt a rush of relief and calm, almost proud, because food was the one thing he could control while everything else felt out of his hands.

qa.q: What was Reena's wise choice, and why?
qa.a: She didn't fight about food but shared her worry and suggested the district hospital doctor, the right place to start.

qa.q: How does Reena see Deepak's behaviour?
qa.a: She sees it as something harmful that scares her, not as stubbornness, and she wants him to get proper help.

grounding: Deepak uses rigid food rules and secret eating to cope with stress and a need for control, finding relief but real harm, and his sister steers him to a doctor.
